| Older backend: test failed with v1 restored | Resolve its error, obtain a fresh preview and repeat the test. No additional source recovery is needed. |
| Recovery required | Restoration or target recovery has not finished. Preserve the evidence and use the job's offered action; do not assume either installation is ready. |
| Migration completed | Validate running v2, downstream paths and playback before resuming normal imports and scans. |

Restoring v1 after a failure does not make the preparation or legacy test successful.
Likewise, a retained archive or an available rollback control does not by itself
mean that recovery is running. Follow the job's result and reported error.

CIFS/SMB shares can finalize file timestamps when an upload closes. Supporting
builds record those closed-file values before later checks; every copied file
still needs complete content verification before local blobs are removed.

A failed input check can identify the source or staged copy, entry type, changed
metadata fields and a digest reference without exposing the original path.
Preserve that reference and the job evidence when reporting a failure; do not
change timestamps, move files or delete retained input to make a check pass.

Bulk migration work has **no fixed overall time limit**. Large file copies,
PostgreSQL dump and restore verification, and native import can take longer on
slow local or network storage. DUMB does not stop a running worker just because
an elapsed-time or inactivity threshold was reached.

After 30 minutes without observable native progress or provider-read activity,
DUMB shows a warning and keeps waiting. A status polling heartbeat or changing
time estimate does not clear that warning; observed progress does. PostgreSQL
steps similarly warn when their activity cannot be observed. A warning is a
reason to review the current stage, not proof that the operation has failed.
Actual process failure, a failed native report or failed verification still
stops acceptance and preserves the recovery path.

A supporting backend offers **Cancel migration** while its current job permits
restoring v1. Use that job's exact confirmation. Cancellation is cooperative:
DUMB records the request and waits for an owned checkpoint. If cancelled before
applications were paused, the job confirms that the source was unchanged; no
restore is needed. Once execution has begun, DUMB stops the contained native
writer and restores v1 before reporting completion. Once the live v2 target has
been exposed and may have accepted writes, cancellation cannot silently restore
v1. Closing the panel does not request cancellation.
A slow or blocked operating-system I/O call can delay a cancellation checkpoint;
wait for the job's confirmed outcome rather than assuming the request completed.
Keep imports, scans and playback stopped while source restoration or recovery runs.

After a controller restart, or if recovery fails, review the retained job's
current authorized actions. A pre-activation job can offer **Restore v1**
(**Rollback** on the older flow) with its exact confirmation to recover v1. A job that still blocks new work takes priority
over newer completed attempts in the migration panel; its current recovery
actions determine what can proceed. Low-space recovery
also requires the selected migration backup location to be mounted and readable.
Keep any expanded legacy input until the job no longer needs it.
Preserve the job files, native report, archives and any retained candidate.
If DUMB cannot confirm that its owned helper stopped, recovery remains held.
Rollback becomes available only after helper termination is confirmed; retain
the private recovery files while reviewing that state.
Deleting a database or job file to clear a lock can destroy the recovery path.

### Recover v2 activation or pending consumers

Starting the live v2 target establishes a different recovery boundary from the
isolated prepared candidate. It may already contain new writes. DUMB retains that target
and the original v1 recovery evidence instead of automatically restoring v1
because a later activation check or downstream start failed.

After native health and the selected delivery mount are verified, DUMB records
the accepted cutover before resuming the previously running consumers. A
consumer start failure leaves that cutover retained and the job held for service
recovery. Review the named failed and pending services and their reported reasons.
Ordered process launch is not proof that every Arr API or playback client is
healthy; verify those separately.

Backends advertising the guarded service recovery controls offer:

- **Verify/restart v2 and retry consumers**, or **Retry pending consumers** after
  accepted cutover. Type the job's displayed confirmation. The backend verifies
  the owned target, current configuration, native health and delivery mount,
  restarting its selected runtime or mount when needed. It then retries only
  the retained pending consumers in dependency order, without repeating the
  import or duplicating already-running services. This action can be available
  while the target still needs verification; a failed verification keeps the hold.
- **Finish with pending services stopped** only when the backend has verified
  the v2 runtime and delivery mount. Review every pending service, acknowledge
  leaving those services stopped and type the separate confirmation. Completion
  retains their warnings and the dashboard reminder after reload. Review their
  errors before starting them later.

If DUMB started with only its recovery control plane, retry or finish can resume
retained services and complete the job before normal background workers have
been initialized. Follow an explicit **restart DUMB** instruction in the job:
restart the container, then refresh status and verify normal startup. The API
marks this condition with `result.restart_required: true`; a completed recovery
job alone does not replace that restart.

Keep media protections and retained evidence while recovery is held. Database
provider changes and old-installation cleanup remain blocked until the held
operation is resolved. Lost mount readiness or uncertain process ownership is
not a successful degraded migration; retain the data and follow the reported
recovery checks.

An older job that already activated v2 can lack the private target-binding
evidence required for these recovery controls. Such a held job needs manual
review of both retained v1 and existing v2 data. Updating DUMB does not invent a
new acceptance receipt or authorize blindly restoring v1; keep both data sets
and the job evidence while resolving its reported blocker.

After a healthy completed cutover, a supporting backend can offer a separate
manual v1 rollback. Its confirmation also requires explicitly accepting the
loss of writes accepted by v2. Preserve any v2 data you need first. This action
restores retained v1 state; it does not merge v2 writes into v1. A held activation
or consumer recovery does not offer this ordinary rollback.

### Review native import omissions

The job's import report distinguishes imported files, omitted files and their
reported reasons. Omitted files are absent from v2; a completed native import does
not establish that those files will be repaired or replaced automatically.

A known, fully accounted source incompatibility can require review before
activation. Read the reasons and affected paths, then explicitly accept the
prepared job's omissions. Acceptance is bound to that candidate's full private
evidence and exact report digest; the dashboard's limited path samples cannot
replace it. Activating the prepared candidate does not run another import.

On the older separate test workflow, cutover can omit the same items or fewer,
including none, when the complete
canonical source media and history census is unchanged. Every remaining omitted
identity, name, path and exact reason must match the reviewed evidence. An item
that succeeds at cutover no longer needs omission consent. New omissions or
changed identities or reasons require another verified review; there is no
generic allowance for a maximum number or percentage of skipped files.

The complete proof also binds referenced metadata and NZB blob contents;
identifiers alone do not establish that those bytes stayed unchanged. Validation
can therefore read many metadata files from the retained source. This proof uses
filesystem reads rather than adding NNTP requests. Keep its full private
evidence with the job; a bounded public sample cannot replace it.
Volatile health scheduling is excluded from this census. Changed source facts
or stale private proof require a fresh preparation and review, or a new test on
an older backend.

A lower count in one native import report is not accepted as a history-loss
tolerance. Every required completed and failed source-history identity must
still exist in the actual v2 database. Unsupported source states, invalid
reserved identities and missing required history remain blockers.

Provider/NNTP failures, unrecognized reasons or report formats, unexplained
missing identities, changed names, database integrity failures and missing
history still block migration. Review provider failures separately from known
source exclusions: the restricted relay can recover missing metadata only when
the configured provider permits the required reads. An acknowledgement does not
override unavailable providers or unexplained omissions.

Supporting builds show **Provider activity** while importing and retain those
observations after the importer stops. Provider numbers follow the captured
provider order. The counts distinguish requests, retries, article-not-found
replies, and connection or protocol errors without showing server addresses or
credentials. Expand **Connection and protocol errors** to see which step failed.
An attempt can recover through a retry or another provider, so these counters
alone do not mean a file was lost. Use the native import report to see whether
any files remain blocked. Older jobs may not contain these observations.

The dashboard bounds its path/reason samples and identifies truncated details;
DUMB retains the full native report privately with the migration job. The
job's report action retrieves that plain-text report through the authenticated
API. Preserve that report and the retained candidate when investigating a
blocked import.
In low-space mode, recovery can need to release the candidate's storage before
restoring v1; the retained archive and diagnostic report remain protected.

## Mount and library continuity

Both mount choices expose InfiniDysk's virtual filesystem. Keeping
`/mnt/debrid/infinidysk` alone is insufficient: existing relative paths such as
`content/<category>/...`, completed-download paths, categories and link semantics
must still identify the same media.

| Mount | Consequences |
|-------|--------------|
| rclone over WebDAV | Native FUSE stays off. DUMB uses the generation 2 HTTP endpoint and Basic login, keeps `--links`, and uses a shorter directory-cache policy because 1.x RC refresh notifications are absent. Rclone settings remain rclone-owned. |
| Native FUSE | Requires working FUSE access, permissions and mount visibility in every consumer namespace. The old associated rclone owner must stop and detach before the native mount takes its exact path. Rclone flags and optimizer recommendations do not apply. |

A foreign, ambiguous, busy or stale mount blocks a transition. DUMB does not
mount over another owner or force-detach a mount to make the check pass. Keep
unrelated rclone instances and shared storage workflows intact.

Before stopping the source, the native FUSE prerequisite check reports missing
`/dev/fuse`, `fusermount3`, or an explicit `user_allow_other` policy in
`/etc/fuse.conf` for a non-root configured mount owner. DUMB's image includes
that policy; review it in a custom image if the check fails. The check does not
edit the policy, detach a stale mount or change unrelated directory ownership.

For symlinks, compare raw targets and verify they resolve through the selected
mount. For STRM files, preserve identity/signing material and the original
reachable origin and signed path. A valid token does not repair a retired URL
route. Generic preview/view links may differ between generations. DUMB's symlink
repair tool does not rewrite STRM URLs.

Choose any later symlink/STRM strategy change separately in InfiniDysk's native
configuration. A global STRM selection still produces symlinks for music and
book jobs. Validate playback from the actual media server/player network;
STRM does not establish compatibility with every media server or remove all
filesystem requirements.

## Native PostgreSQL conversion

After activating generation 2 and validating the running installation, open
**Tools → InfiniDysk 2 database
conversion**. This uses the native copy, synchronization and cutover engine,
not DUMB's generation 1 SQLite-to-PostgreSQL adapter.

1. Have an administrator create and start a dedicated, empty PostgreSQL database
   with **`C` collation** and a suitable owner role first. DUMB's managed option
   uses its configured PostgreSQL connection; it does not create the named
   database. The ordinary [database list](../services/dependent/postgres.md)
   inherits the cluster's locale and does not request `C` explicitly. Use the
   destination example below, then select that database or supply its external
   TCP address and TLS policy. The migration preview only verifies the destination.
2. Preview the destination. Review its physical cluster identity, database OID
   and schema, along with source, emptiness and recovery checks.
3. Confirm backups and the destination reset acknowledgement, type the exact
   confirmation, then start native copying and synchronization.
4. Wait for the backend to advertise **cutover**. Review and confirm that action
   separately. The native restart may retain its process ID; wait for confirmed
   provider state and service health.

### Prepare a PostgreSQL destination

The conversion needs a separate, empty PostgreSQL database with DUMB's supported `C` locale. Selecting managed PostgreSQL fills connection settings; it does not create that destination for you. Ask the person managing PostgreSQL to prepare it, then enter the same database name and role in the conversion form. Keep the existing v1 database and every other application's database intact.

<details class="geek-details" markdown="1">
<summary>Technical alternative: create the dedicated PostgreSQL destination with SQL</summary>

The following PostgreSQL 16 example creates a **new** database with an explicit
locale. Connect as a database administrator to a maintenance database such as
`postgres`, and run the statement outside a transaction. Replace
`example_role` with the existing role that the conversion will use; for
DUMB-managed PostgreSQL this is its configured `postgres.user`. Choose an unused
database name and enter that same name in the conversion form.

```sql
CREATE DATABASE infinidysk_v2
  OWNER "example_role"
  TEMPLATE template0
  ENCODING 'UTF8'
  LOCALE_PROVIDER libc
  LC_COLLATE 'C'
  LC_CTYPE 'C';
```

`template0` permits an explicit locale even when the cluster was initialized
with another default. Adding an ordinary database-list entry alone can inherit
`C.UTF-8`, which differs from DUMB's supported exact-`C` destination contract.
Do not change an existing cluster's locale or drop/recreate an existing database
to make the preview pass. Select a separate, empty destination; retain the old
v1 database and all other applications' databases.

InfiniDysk's native tool can warn and continue with other collations; DUMB's
guarded workflow requires `C` so its supported destination keeps the intended
folder ordering and path-search behavior. See PostgreSQL's
[CREATE DATABASE reference](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createdatabase.html)
and the native [PostgreSQL preparation guide](https://www.infinidysk.com/v2/operate/postgresql/).
</details>

Successful playback after the major upgrade verifies the current SQLite-backed
installation. It does not establish that this separate PostgreSQL destination
exists or is reachable. SQLite remains current while native copying and
synchronization run; PostgreSQL is selected only after confirmed cutover.

### Destination preview problems

Preview failures concern the selected PostgreSQL destination. Resolve the
reported condition, then request and review a fresh preview:

| Reported condition | Next step |
| --- | --- |
| The destination database does not exist | Create the new empty database first, using the same name and role as the conversion form. Selecting managed PostgreSQL reuses its connection settings. |
| PostgreSQL rejects the credentials | Check the configured role, password and PostgreSQL connection/authentication policy. Keep credentials out of screenshots and shared logs. |
| Physical identity inspection is denied | Ask the database administrator to review the named permission in the destination database. Keep the identity check enabled. |
| The destination could not be verified | Check that the server is running and listening, the address/port and database name are correct, and the connection and TLS policies permit DUMB's selected connection. |
| The database does not satisfy DUMB's `C`-collation or emptiness checks | Prepare a different dedicated destination with the supported locale. Keep the existing database intact. |

<details class="geek-details" markdown="1">
<summary>Technical alternative: grant a specifically denied identity-inspection function</summary>

Ordinary PostgreSQL roles can normally execute the catalog identity function.
If an administrator has revoked it and the preview explicitly reports that
denial, the administrator can grant only the required function in the
**destination database**, using the role selected for conversion:

```sql
GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION pg_catalog.pg_control_system()
  TO "example_role";
```

This does not require making the application role a superuser. A successful
login alone does not establish that DUMB can verify the destination's physical
identity and safety requirements. PostgreSQL documents the
[control data functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-info.html#FUNCTIONS-CONTROLDATA)
and [function privileges](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-priv.html).
</details>

### Copy, cutover and recovery

External credentials are sent only to the private backend preview and cleared
from the form. They are not returned in public status or browser job storage.
The backend checks the current job and physical source/target identities before
each destructive action; a changed target or stale preview blocks it.

!!! warning "Dedicated destination required"

    Native cancellation can empty the migration destination's tables. Never
    use a database belonging to another application or reuse the source as the
    destination. Cancel and rollback are offered only when their current
    backend guards permit them; do not call upstream cleanup routes to bypass
    those checks.

The native **cancel** and retained **rollback** actions require their own exact
confirmation and acknowledgements. Rollback restores retained SQLite state; it
does not merge later PostgreSQL writes. A fresh 2.x deployment configured directly
through `INFINIDYSK_DATABASE_URL` is environment-managed and disables the native
provider conversion UI. Do not use that variable to convert an existing store.

Cancellation can complete with a nonblocking **native cleanup needs review**
notice while SQLite remains active. Retained private warnings can concern
PostgreSQL destination tables or SQLite change-capture cleanup. Review that
evidence under `/config/migrations/infinidysk-v2-postgres` before reusing the
destination or changing capture state. The private bundle also contains
connection credentials. If the native
warning calls for a restart, use a normal managed restart after reviewing it;
do not delete tables or provider files to clear the notice. A nonempty destination
still fails a later preview.

Rollback can restore the retained SQLite source while PostgreSQL is unreachable.
DUMB records the restored file identity before restarting it. If mount recovery
is delayed, retrying verifies that same SQLite file and its health without
restoring over writes accepted since the first restart. A missing or replaced
file remains blocked for investigation.

## Existing Arr download-client credentials

For a new v1-to-v2 migration, DUMB carries the effective v1 **SAB-compatible
download API key** into v2 and verifies it before accepting the candidate. This
includes supported v1 environment key overrides. The native v2 administrative
API key is a separate credential; do not substitute it into an Arr SAB download
client.

Whole-section JSON overrides such as `INFINIDYSK__SAB` are refused during
v1-to-v2 migration: native section replacement can hide the retained download API
key. Remove that override or express the settings as individual
`INFINIDYSK__SAB__...` fields. An explicit `INFINIDYSK__SAB__API_KEY` must match
the retained v1 key; other individual SAB fields remain supported. If DUMB
requests renewed key proof, generate and review a fresh preview, then prepare a
new candidate. An older backend requires its separate test before migration.

DUMB does not edit Arr applications' settings. If v2 is already running after an
earlier migration or manual credential changes, compare the Arr download client's
host, port and SAB API key with the current v2 configuration, then test that
client's connection. Updating DUMB does not automatically rotate working v2 or
Arr credentials back to the retained v1 key.

## Authentication with the retained backend port

When `backend_port` differs from `frontend_port`, DUMB runs a compatibility
relay so existing SAB, WebDAV and signed-stream URLs can retain their port.
The relay cannot preserve the original network peer identity, so DUMB locks
native **Required** authentication at launch while it is enabled. Native **Local** or
**Disabled** exemptions cannot be used through this relay.

The wizard reports this policy, and the native settings UI shows the
DUMB-enforced authentication lock. Explicit conflicting `INFINIDYSK__AUTH__MODE`
overrides are rejected before installation or migration. DUMB does not rewrite
the saved native authentication setting; the runtime override keeps it inactive
while compatibility forwarding is enabled, including after native UI/API changes.

To use native authentication policy without this relay, configure matching
backend and frontend ports. Review and update existing client and stream origins
before removing the old port. Authentication requirements on the native listener
then follow its own configuration.

## Validate and recover

Before resuming normal work, verify queue/history/provider settings, timezone,
login and OIDC policy, virtual categories, existing symlinks, representative
file/range/seek reads, signed STRM playback and paths from each real consumer.
Run a deliberate test import only after those checks and review the resulting
Arr and media-server paths. A healthy process or a successful fixture test is
not proof of real provider/account playback.

InfiniDysk 2 uses a dedicated root URL for its UI. Use the direct local address
or configured public portal; embedded subpath login/playback remains unavailable
unless the backend explicitly advertises a validated adapter.

If the job is interrupted or needs recovery, keep the original data, any exposed
v2 target and private job evidence under `/config/migrations/infinidysk-v2`.
Use the offered action for that recovery boundary: retrying v2 service recovery
keeps the target, while an authorized v1 rollback restores retained v1 state.
Post-cutover rollback requires accepting discarded v2 writes; those writes are
not copied back. A failed rollback or unavailable recovery action needs
investigation before restarting imports, scans or services. Do not delete
retained state to clear a banner.

## Retire the old v1 installation

After a verified cutover and real-library validation, the same migration panel
can offer **Retire the old v1 installation** for a migration that retained the
original local tree. Low-space migrations have already reused that data and do
not offer original-tree retirement. Their recovery archive remains separate from
temporary migration copies; keep it for recovery.
Keep independent backups and confirm successful playback and a test import
before retiring a retained local installation.

1. Select **Review old-installation cleanup** and review the exact old paths,
   estimated reclaim and retained backups.
2. Confirm playback, test-import and rollback-retirement acknowledgements, then
   type the server's exact confirmation.
3. Select **Retire rollback and remove reviewed v1 files** and follow the job.

Cleanup verifies the retained source backup and unchanged v1 files, then durably
retires automated major rollback before removing reviewed entries. Backups and
receipts remain retained; PostgreSQL databases, shared mounts and unrelated
libraries are not removed. Later v2 writes are never merged into a v1 backup.

If cleanup stops, the old tree can be partially removed and automated rollback
stays retired. Preserve the job and deletion-manifest evidence; use a fresh
review to resume the same removal plan. Changed files or mounts stop remaining
removal, and new files are retained rather than added to the deletion plan.
Do not delete backups or job state to clear a cleanup warning.

See [Process Management API](../api/process.md#infinidysk-2-workflows),
[Media Library Protection](media-library-protection.md),
[Symlink Operations](symlinks.md) and the
[generation 1 PostgreSQL migration guide](arr-postgres-migration.md) for the
separate existing workflows.

---

Source: https://dumbarr.com/dev/features/install-cache/

# Install cache and safe updates

DUMB keeps reproducible downloads, package-manager data, and selected compiled
service artifacts under `/config/.cache/dumb`. The cache accelerates container
startup, updates, and exact-source reinstalls without treating a cached file as
trusted merely because it already exists.

Service configuration, databases, media, symlinks, credentials, and active
runtime directories are not cache entries.

<details class="geek-details" markdown="1">
<summary>Technical details: persistent-path exclusions during updates</summary>

Destructive update clears are built from guarded exclusions rather than trusting
only the saved `exclude_dirs` list. DUMB automatically preserves an in-tree
service config file, explicit config/data/database paths, conventional persistent
data/database directories, root-level SQLite files and their active sidecars,
and symlinked data directories. The guarded paths are also excluded from archive
merges, while replaceable source and runtime output can still be refreshed.


</details>

## Use the cache controls

Open **Dashboard → Updates → Install cache** when supported by your backend. Check usage and fallback state, then choose an action deliberately:

| Task | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Check cached downloads | Verify downloads |
| Reclaim rebuildable space | Prune to limit |
| Force a runtime rebuild next time | Clear build artifacts |
| Change the managed size target | Save the limit, then prune separately if desired |

After an action finishes, check its result and refresh the displayed usage. These actions do not stop services or delete active runtimes. Removing warm caches can make the next install slower. If an update is already active, wait for it to finish.

## Installing a configured release

For services using the shared release installer, an explicit configured-target
install applies the selected fixed release even when automatic updates are enabled
or that release is already installed. Scheduled setup still respects release pins;
saving a release selector alone does not request a reinstall.

For the frontend task, open the service's **Tools → Updates**, review its saved target, and select **Install configured release** when offered. Wait for completion and check service health. See [Auto-update](auto-update.md#install-a-saved-release-branch-or-commit).

Services with dedicated source installers retain their own installation behavior.
Manual installs continue to use the existing snapshot and failure-recovery flow.
A failed release download is reported as an installation failure, rather than a
successful restart of the existing version.

<details class="geek-details" markdown="1">
<summary>Technical details: verified candidate activation and rollback</summary>

## Safety model

An external project can always fail to download or build. DUMB's goal is to
make that failure non-destructive:

1. Resolve the requested release, branch head, or exact commit.
2. Download into a content-addressed cache and verify its SHA-256 digest.
   For GitHub release assets, also require the published SHA-256 digest when
   available. Conditional requests and offline reuse still check that published
   digest before accepting cached content.
3. Validate the complete archive before applying files. Unsafe paths, links,
   malformed archives, extraction errors, and configured size limits fail the
   installation.
4. Build and verify the replacement runtime.
5. Stop the old process only when the replacement is ready where the service
   layout supports candidate activation.
6. Start the replacement and require it to remain healthy for the configured
   stabilization period.
7. Restore the previous runtime automatically if activation or health
   stabilization fails.

Traefik Proxy Admin uses full same-filesystem candidate activation. Other
source-built services retain a rollback snapshot of replaceable runtime files
while their persistent paths stay in place. Services whose package manager or
database owns the upgrade transaction keep their existing service-specific
recovery behavior.
</details>

!!! warning "Application database migrations"

    A runtime rollback cannot safely undo every application-owned database
    migration. DUMB never replaces persistent data with a cached copy. If an
    upstream migration is not backward compatible, leave the restored service
    stopped and follow that application's documented database recovery path.

If an archive install fails and restoring a previous file also fails, DUMB
keeps the recovery backup and reports its location. Preserve that backup until
the service's files have been recovered. Further archive installs and automatic
directory clears stop while a recovery workspace remains, so a retry cannot
erase that evidence. A failure to remove backups after a successful install is
reported separately and does not undo the new runtime.

<details class="geek-details" markdown="1">
<summary>Technical details: publisher signatures, checksums, and trust roots</summary>

## Download verification

DUMB uses different checks for different download sources:

| Download | Verification |
| --- | --- |
| Managed Bun runtime | Verify the publisher-signed checksum manifest against a bundled, pinned Bun key, then check the selected ZIP's SHA-256 before extraction or execution. |
| Local .NET SDK bootstrap | Verify Microsoft's installer-script signature against its bundled, pinned key before running the script to resolve an SDK version. Check the SDK archive's SHA-512 against official Microsoft HTTPS release metadata before extraction or execution. |
| Shared GitHub release assets | Check the selected asset's published SHA-256 digest when the release API supplies it, including cached and offline reuse. |
| Ubuntu packages, including Tini | Use APT's authenticated repository metadata and package checksums. |

A required Bun or Microsoft signature that is missing, invalid, or signed by an
unrecognized key stops provisioning. Checksum mismatches also stop provisioning.
The existing Bun binary or local .NET SDK stays in place until a verified
candidate passes its version check. DUMB does not retry these failures with an
unsigned installer or trust a replacement key automatically.

Some GitHub release assets have no published digest. Those remain installable
with HTTPS and DUMB's cache integrity checks; the log explicitly reports the
missing published checksum. A present but malformed or unsupported digest
refuses the download. A cache's own checksum detects changed cached bytes,
but does not establish who originally published them.

Published SDK and GitHub checksums provide integrity checks, rather than a
separate publisher signature. OCI digests and package-manager lockfile hashes
also do not imply universal publisher-signature or provenance verification.
Bundled signing keys need maintenance when their publishers announce rotations
or revocations; verification does not fetch new trust roots at runtime.
</details>

<details class="geek-details" markdown="1">
<summary>Technical details: cache paths, limits, and ownership</summary>

## Configuration

```json
{
  "dumb": {
    "install_cache": {
      "enabled": true,
      "path": "/config/.cache/dumb",
      "max_size_gib": 25,
      "artifact_retention_count": 2,
      "clean_retry": true,
      "max_download_size_mb": 4096,
      "max_archive_entries": 250000,
      "max_unpacked_size_gib": 50,
      "activation_health_timeout_seconds": 120,
      "activation_stabilization_seconds": 15
    }
  }
}
```

Keep the cache on persistent local storage when possible. It may reside on a
different filesystem from service runtimes. The shared archive installer
stages extracted files and rollback backups on the service's filesystem,
including directly mounted service directories, so file activation uses atomic
same-filesystem renames. Allow enough free space there for the candidate and
temporary backups. DUMB refuses broad system/data roots such as
`/`, `/config`, `/data`, and `/mnt` as the cache root and falls back to the
default cache directory.

The cache is owned by the DUMB controller rather than managed service users.
If the cache root or one of its managed namespaces is recursively `chown`ed,
DUMB validates the tree and restores controller ownership before the next
cache operation. The repair removes group/other write permission while
preserving executable bits required by cached runtimes. It does not follow
symlinks or cross a nested mount inside the cache tree.

If the configured cache is a symlink, has an unsupported file type, contains
an unexpected nested mount during ownership repair, or cannot be repaired due
to filesystem permissions, DUMB leaves active runtimes untouched and uses a
new controller-only cache under `/tmp` for the current process. The dashboard
shows this fallback and its reason. Correct the configured path or ownership
and restart DUMB to resume the persistent cache; the temporary fallback is not
reused after restart.

</details>

<details class="geek-details" markdown="1">
<summary>Technical details: package-manager cache behavior</summary>

## Package-manager behavior

- pnpm uses a shared content-addressed store grouped by pnpm major, verifies
  store integrity, and attempts a frozen lockfile install first. A lockfile
  compatibility retry is allowed only after pnpm specifically reports a
  lockfile mismatch; it remains inside the rollback-protected install phase.
- Python services receive a clean virtual environment. pip and Poetry share
  download caches by Python ABI and architecture, and DUMB runs `pip check`
  before accepting the environment.
- NuGet packages are shared by architecture. Projects with
  `packages.lock.json` restore in locked mode; publish remains `--no-restore`.
- Go module and build caches are persistent and architecture-scoped.
- Bun, Yarn, and Deno retain persistent shared caches and use immutable/frozen
  lock behavior when their project supplies a lockfile.
- mediastorm OCI data remains digest-addressed and verified.

</details>

## Dashboard maintenance

Newer backends advertise `install_cache_management`. The dashboard **Updates**
panel then shows three distinct totals:

- **Managed cache** is the current `/config/.cache/dumb` tree and is the value
  governed by `max_size_gib`.
- **Legacy release caches** are exact DUMB-owned package-manager locations
  discovered from older releases.
- **Combined install cache** is the complete managed plus legacy disk usage.

The panel also shows current namespace sizes and actions to:

- save a managed-cache limit from 1 through 1024 GiB when the backend advertises
  `install_cache_limit_settings`;
- verify downloaded objects and quarantine corrupt entries;
- prune least-recently-used entries down to the configured limit; and
- clear compiled artifacts so the next reinstall performs a clean build.

Backends that additionally advertise `install_cache_cleanup` expose a
user-directed cleanup selector. It can remove only legacy caches, quarantine,
compiled artifacts, verified downloads, dependency caches, or all rebuildable
cache. Every scope requires confirmation. DUMB accepts named scopes rather
than filesystem paths, re-discovers legacy entries immediately before
deletion, and refuses symlinked, mounted, or moved paths. Maintenance returns
HTTP 409 until startup completes and while DUMB's service-update lock is active.

Saving the limit persists `dumb.install_cache.max_size_gib`. It does not delete
anything immediately. Select **Prune to limit** when you want DUMB to reclaim
least-recently-used rebuildable cache entries down to the new target. This split
prevents an accidental number change from immediately removing a warm cache.

Legacy discovery covers the old per-project pnpm/Bun buckets, Maintainerr Yarn
cache, Profilarr Deno cache, and DUMB-created per-service pip, Poetry, and NuGet
package caches. It does not classify generic application cache directories as
install cache, and it preserves the current Traefik Proxy Admin runtime data
that still intentionally lives below `/config/.pnpm-store`.

The frontend hides the entire section for APIs without
`install_cache_management` and independently hides scoped cleanup unless
`install_cache_cleanup=true`. The editable limit is independently gated by
`install_cache_limit_settings=true`, so a newer frontend does not submit the
new nested config field to an older backend schema.

Pruning and clearing artifacts never stop services or remove active runtimes.
Cleaning downloads or dependency caches makes later installs slower until the
cache warms again. DUMB serializes these actions against managed updates, but
operators should still avoid cleanup while another install path is actively
building.
Do not manually delete transaction journals or `dumb-previous` directories
while an update is active.

## Recovery guidance

If an update reports that the previous runtime was restored:

1. Confirm that the service is running and inspect its service log.
2. Open **Updates → Install cache** and run **Verify downloads**.
3. Use **Clear build artifacts** if the failure points to missing or invalid
   compiled output.
4. Retry the update. DUMB will reuse valid dependency downloads but rebuild the
   service runtime.
5. If rollback itself failed, do not repeatedly update. Preserve the service
   directory and logs, then restore the application's data from its normal
   backup process.

---

Source: https://dumbarr.com/dev/features/installation-backups/

# Installation backup and restore

Open **Settings → Backups and restore** to manage installation archives and
shared backup destinations. This requires a backend advertising installation
backup protocol `1`; older backends continue to expose their existing tools.

## Choose a task

| Task | Start here |
| --- | --- |
| Make an archive | [Create a backup](#create-a-backup) |
| Keep a recurring archive | [Schedule backups](#schedule-backups) |
| Recover an installation | [Restore an existing or fresh installation](#restore-an-existing-or-fresh-installation) |
| Resolve a held startup | [Startup and private recovery state](#startup-and-private-recovery-state) |

Review coverage and storage before the first backup. Archives contain credentials and keys, and are not encrypted.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Settings[Open Settings Backups and restore] --> Choose[Choose destination and archive format]
    Choose --> Preview[Preview backup and review coverage]
    Preview --> Confirm[Confirm downtime and backup]
    Confirm --> Wait[Wait for verification and service resume]
    Wait --> Check[Check saved archive and application access]
```

## What an installation backup contains

The preview inventories DUMB configuration, authentication and signing state,
managed application configuration and persistent data, managed databases, and
configured symlink state. Existing data belonging to disabled services is
included when it is discovered. Review the actual roots and exclusions rather
than assuming that a process's working directory is its complete data directory.

Plex DBRepair's native installation and database directories are included from
the nested `plex.dbrepair` settings when they exist, including when scheduled
repair is disabled. The default installation directory is `/data/dbrepair`.
Its supported `install_dir` and `databases_path` settings supplement the
existing Plex database coverage; see the
[Plex configuration guide](../services/core/plex-media-server.md). A command's
working directory alone does not add its contents to the archive.

Media content, mounted remote libraries, external services and databases,
container images, host deployment files and separate log/cache stores are outside
the installation archive. Application-owned logs, artwork, blob stores and caches
inside an included data root may still be included. Preserve your Compose/Portainer deployment, bind mounts
and external systems separately. A symlink's target text is preserved without
copying the referenced media. Recognized STRM, subtitle, metadata and artwork
sidecars in managed library-link directories are included. Actual media files
and unrecognized regular payloads in those directories remain blockers; DUMB
identifies the path instead of silently omitting it. DUMB refuses unsupported
or ambiguous state instead of silently reporting a complete backup.

<details class="geek-details" markdown="1">
<summary>Technical details: aliases, archive metadata, and unsupported file types</summary>

A managed file or selected service alias is archived as a literal entry, so a
final symlink is preserved without copying its target. A sibling alias under
`data_root` pointing to an already-covered managed directory is also preserved
as literal link state; its target is not copied again. Archive storage
locations and intermediate directories must still be verifiable without
following symlinks. An ancestry error identifies the component that failed and
the reason; clearing it must not require deleting or retargeting service aliases.

Both supported archive formats preserve regular files, directories, literal symlinks,
normal POSIX ownership/permissions and modification times. Hardlinks are stored
as independent files. Extended attributes, ACLs, special permission bits and
unresolved nested mounts are blockers. Nested controller-auth paths or an
inventory that exceeds the restorable transaction budget also require review;
the utility does not silently discard that state.


</details>

Archives contain credentials and private keys and are not encrypted.
Restrict access to the destination, partial exports and downloaded copies;
shared storage permission consent does not prove confidentiality.

## Choose storage

In **Backup destination**, expand **Register a backup destination**.
Register an existing container-visible directory, then explicitly select that
destination or **Use global default**. The separate **Global default** controls
show, set or clear the saved preference. See
[Backup storage](backup-storage.md) for registration and mount requirements.

An already-mounted NFS/SMB directory can hold closed archives when it passes the
storage checks. Enable **Allow shared archive permissions** during registration
only when you trust the destination's access controls; it starts unchecked and
restrictive POSIX checks remain the default.
DUMB does not mount shares or change their existing ownership/permissions.
Active database and private recovery working files remain local. A missing or
replaced destination mount blocks the operation;
DUMB does not write into an underlying local directory as a fallback.

A configured backup profile cannot use a managed persistence root itself or a
directory containing one. This includes unselected or disabled profiles:
excluding such a backup location would hide application state from the archive.
Review the reported paths and correct the conflicting profile. A separate
destination or a dedicated child archive directory can still be used when it
passes the storage checks.

## Choose an archive format

Uncompressed `.tar` is the default. When the backend supports Zstandard,
manual backups and the schedule can each select compressed `.tar.zst` archives.
Choose the format before requesting a preview; changing it requires a new
review. Older backends retain uncompressed backups.

Zstandard streams directly to the selected destination without making a
complete uncompressed archive on local disk first. Compression can reduce
storage and transfer volume, but requires CPU time and may save little for
already-compressed data. It does not encrypt the archive or make shared storage
private. Each archive remains a complete, standalone backup; compression adds
neither incremental backups nor deduplication.

Capacity checks remain conservative: they reserve an uncompressed archive
estimate plus overhead, without assuming a compression ratio. A preview can
therefore block for space even if the actual compressed output might fit.
Local inventory/verification ledgers and restore staging still require their
own working space.

DUMB verifies the stored archive bytes and the complete logical contents before
publishing either format. Restore detects compression from the file contents,
not its filename; existing uncompressed archives remain supported.

## Create a backup

Plan for application downtime. Once DUMB stops managed applications, playback, imports, scans, and service UIs remain unavailable until archive checks and service resume finish. The API and frontend stay available through their direct ports. Large data sets or slow storage can take hours; there is no promised finish time.

Use direct frontend/API access before starting. Managed proxies and tunnels can stop with the applications, making their public routes unavailable.

1. Select a destination and archive format in **Settings → Backups and restore**.
2. Choose **Preview backup** to review roots, exclusions, estimated space, and blockers while applications remain running.
3. Stop external writers, including another container sharing the same state.
4. Review the downtime, credential-handling, and external-state acknowledgements, enter the displayed phrase, and select **Start reviewed backup**.
5. Follow the admitted job through archive verification and service resume.
6. Check both the saved archive receipt and application availability before leaving the operation.

On backends advertising `installation_backup_direct_start`, **Back up without preview** skips the live file/size census. It still requires the acknowledgements. DUMB checks coverage, stops the previously running applications, and uses one cold inventory for capacity and archiving. A reviewed start also uses this cold inventory rather than repeating a full live census. Scheduled backups use the same direct path.

If capacity is insufficient, the operation fails before archive payload is written and attempts to resume applications. Measured capacity, required space, and missing space are shown when supported. An admitted scheduled failure waits for its normal interval; transient admission blockers can retry after five minutes.

### Follow progress and confirm the result

The application-wide notice survives navigation and refresh. **Preparing installation backup** describes the admission recheck before an archive job is accepted; it does not mean applications have already stopped. After admission, the job reports its current stage and elapsed time.

Do not stop DUMB or its host while the operation is active. A lost connection or proxy timeout does not prove failure or cancellation. Reconnect through the direct frontend/API and refresh status before submitting another operation. Direct-start retries retain their request identity, and a consumed preview cannot start a second job.

| Result | Meaning and next action |
| --- | --- |
| Archive verified and saved | Source consistency, logical archive checks, stored-byte readback, and catalog publication passed; service resume may still be running |
| Completed | Review the receipt and verify resumed application health |
| Archive saved, recovery required | Keep the receipt; use **Finish backup recovery** to resume services rather than repeating the backup |
| Failed before publication | Partial output is not a verified backup; follow the recovery guidance |
| Publication interrupted / unconfirmed | Inspect the catalog and recovery details before assuming an archive exists or is absent |

DUMB resumes only applications that were running before the backup, in dependency order, with storage mounts ready before their consumers. Previously stopped services remain stopped. A failed resume does not invalidate an already verified and catalogued archive.

<details class="geek-details" markdown="1">
<summary>Technical details: progress phases and consistency checks</summary>

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Admit[Validate operation and reserve persistence] --> Stop[Stop previously running writers]
    Stop --> Inventory[Inventory stable source]
    Inventory --> Archive[Stream archive to destination]
    Archive --> Verify[Check source and read back archive]
    Verify --> Publish[Publish archive and catalog receipt]
    Publish --> Resume[Resume prior services in dependency order]
```

| Phase | What its counters measure |
| --- | --- |
| Inventorying | Entries and logical source sizes; no archive transfer |
| Archiving | Stored archive stream, including headers, padding, and manifest |
| Checking source | A second source read/hash pass to detect changed data |
| Verifying | Readback of the stored archive |

For Zstandard, archive-stream bytes are compressed stored bytes. Source-size and hash counters are uncompressed file data. Counters reset between phases; a percentage describes only a phase with a known total. It is not an overall percentage or a reliable finish-time estimate. A phase reaching its total can still leave later checks and service resume outstanding.

Worker timestamps report actual work updates. Polling status does not itself advance inventory or transfer progress. Older backends can show only stage and elapsed time.

Seerr Sync and Metrics storage operations reserve installation persistence for their complete operations, including SQLite connection cleanup. A busy cycle can delay admission. During the backup hold, those controller writes pause and resume through their normal schedules after the hold ends.

There is no fixed overall file-count or payload-size ceiling. Individual path, nesting, record, metadata, and restorable-transaction checks still apply. Local space is needed for verification ledgers and later restore staging in addition to archive capacity. A large NAS destination does not remove those requirements.

Database consistency requires a stopped [PostgreSQL cluster](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/backup-file.html) and quiescent [SQLite databases and journals](https://sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html#_backup_or_restore_while_a_transaction_is_active).

</details>

### If service resume needs attention

Follow the job's exact recovery action and verify the affected service's logs before retrying a backup. For PostgreSQL, a literal `{postgres_config_dir}` in a launch error indicates an older launcher that failed to expand its configured placeholders; it is separate from archive consistency. Update through the normal image path and preserve existing database state.

A pgAdmin connection-registration warning can require account or connection review even when its web service is running. DUMB preserves existing accounts/definitions; it does not replace them to clear the warning.

A successful archive checksum describes recorded bytes. Keep an independent copy and rehearse restore before relying on the archive for disaster recovery.

### Follow or cancel a backup preview

On backends with tracked backup-preview support, the progress notice shows the
current stage and managed root, entries scanned, logical bytes inventoried and
elapsed time. These are inventory counters, not bytes already copied to an
archive. DUMB does not show a percentage or remaining-time estimate before it
knows the complete scope. A quiet counter while a filesystem call is pending
does not by itself mean that the scan failed.

You can leave Settings and return, or refresh the browser, to reconnect to the
same preview while the DUMB controller remains running. The interface checks
its retained status and result rather than automatically starting another scan.
Completion is reported with the same notification style as a user-run update;
review the returned blockers and capacity report before confirming a backup.

**Cancel preview** requests a cooperative stop. Wait until the status reports
**Cancelled**: an in-flight filesystem operation can need time to return, and
the temporary local inventory must be cleaned up before the scan releases its
lock. Cancellation does not stop applications, create an archive or remove
application files. Closing the tab alone does not request cancellation.

Preview tracking is held by the running controller, not a resumable disk job.
After a DUMB restart, request a new preview explicitly. A completed review's
15-minute confirmation window begins after the scan finishes, not when scanning
starts. There is no fixed scan-duration limit.

Starting the confirmed backup rechecks the reviewed coverage. With direct-start support, DUMB does not repeat the complete live file census; its later cold inventory supplies the authoritative size. Older backends can repeat a longer live recheck. The preparation notice reconnects after refresh, and archive-job progress starts after admission.

Older backends keep the synchronous preview flow. Its spinner and elapsed time
indicate a pending request, but cannot provide scan counters, reconnection or
cancellation. Keep that page open to receive its result; refreshing it does not
reliably stop the backend scan.

Estimates are not a reservation: another process can consume space afterward.
Admission is checked again during the operation, and failed or incomplete
output is never advertised as a verified backup.

If the connection drops after a start request, the operation may already have
been accepted. Reconnect through direct frontend/API access and refresh status
before submitting another operation. Keep the recorded job identity when one
was received.

The archive list reports completed archives separately from running or failed
jobs. Record the selected archive and retain an independent copy before relying
on it for disaster recovery. A checksum verifies the recorded bytes; a successful
restore rehearsal remains the practical test of your recovery procedure.

### Cancel a running backup

On backends advertising backup cancellation, **Cancel backup** requests a
cooperative stop for a manual or scheduled installation backup. Keep the
container running and wait for **Cancelled**. An in-flight filesystem or network
operation can take time to return before the worker reaches a cancellation
checkpoint.

This job control becomes available after admission. The earlier coverage and
capacity recheck has not stopped applications or admitted an archive job, so it
does not offer that job's cancel action. Closing the page does not cancel a
submitted start request; keep monitoring its preparation and accepted job state.

DUMB stops archive work, removes only the unpublished output owned by that job,
and attempts to resume the previously running applications in dependency order.
It does not restore an archive or replace application data. Existing completed
archives remain available. If services cannot resume safely, the job reports
**Recovery required** and retains its recovery evidence instead of claiming that
cancellation restored service availability.

Cancellation closes before the verified archive is published. The control is
unavailable once the job has passed that boundary, after completion, and for
installation restores. Closing the browser does not cancel a job. Older backends
can expose **Cancel preview** without supporting cancellation of an actual
backup; those are separate operations.

## Unclassified data in a backup preview

A preview can stop on an unrecognized child of `data_root`, even when that
directory is empty. Current backends identify the first unclassified path and
entry type in the blocker; long or unusual paths are escaped and can be marked
as truncated. The backup job has not started and managed services have not
been stopped.

The inventory follows supported application persistence settings. There is no
generic application/media classification wizard or arbitrary include/exclude
switch for this guard. Review the reported path and its owning service's
actual configuration. Do not add unrelated settings, rename, move or delete
state just to clear the warning. If an existing DUMB-managed path is missing
from coverage, retain it and report its path and owning tool so that its
persistence can be qualified. Custom state and external media require their
own backup/deployment review; DUMB does not silently omit them or sweep them
into an installation archive.

## Schedule backups

Scheduling is off by default. Enable it deliberately, choose its destination,
interval, archive format and retention, then select **Save backup schedule**. Check the next scheduled run and use **Reload saved schedule** to verify the saved choices. The schedule
keeps its own format choice; changing a manual backup does not change it.
Each manual or scheduled run
creates a full, standalone archive; incremental or deduplicated installation
backups are not currently supported. Scheduled backups use the same
coverage, quiescence, admission and verification checks as manual backups, so
schedule them during a suitable maintenance window.

Saving or enabling a schedule requires reviewing the same downtime warning as
a manual backup. Every scheduled run stops the managed applications until its
backup and resume stages finish, which may extend beyond the intended window.
The global backup notice shows scheduled activity too. Changing or disabling
the schedule does not cancel an already-running job; use that job's supported
**Cancel backup** control and wait for its terminal result.

Missed or blocked jobs remain visible. A schedule does not bypass startup,
another active operation, unavailable storage or insufficient space. Retention
applies only to verified scheduled installation archives owned by that schedule;
manual archives and other tools' backups are retained separately.

## Restore an existing or fresh installation

A restore replaces managed state and requires downtime. Keep a separate backup
of the current installation and keep external writers stopped throughout the
operation, including any other DUMB container using the same mounted state.
Restore only archives whose origin you trust.

1. Provision the required container image and original container-visible mounts.
   For a fresh installation, open the backup/restore entry before rerunning
   onboarding or enabling application services.
2. Select a catalogued archive, or enter the container-visible path of an
   installation archive already mounted into the container. The mounted-file
   option does not require the old installation's local catalog receipts.
   If that file has fixed/shared permissions, review its origin and access
   controls before enabling **Allow shared archive permissions**. This is an
   independent checkbox for the mounted file and starts unchecked.
   Catalogued archives use their registered destination's permission policy.
3. Request a restore preview. Review archive integrity, application data roots,
   container/database compatibility, destination identity, space requirements,
   and any existing data that would be replaced.
4. Complete the displayed acknowledgements and confirmation phrase, then start.
5. Follow the retained job. After a successful restore, restart the container
   when instructed so DUMB reloads the restored configuration and authentication.
6. Verify login, mounts, application databases, imports and playback before
   retiring the independent backup.

The restore cannot recreate host mounts or a missing external database.
Incompatible paths, architecture or database state are blockers. Restored
authentication can require the original installation's login after restart.
Keep the original registry image digest with your deployment files; archive
compatibility metadata does not recreate or pin the container image itself.

Restore preview reads and verifies the complete archive. Large NAS archives can
take several minutes; the interface reports verification in progress and does
not automatically submit another request. This read-only phase does not stop
applications. Restore staging is also verified before managed writers are stopped
and live state is replaced.

Archives are checked before extraction into private local staging. Paths,
checksums and file types are validated; archive links cannot direct extraction
outside that staging tree. The restore retains rollback evidence for replaced
state. Where a job advertises **Rollback**, the control is available only after
an eligible completed, failed or recovery-required state; it cannot run while
that job is queued or running. This is recovery of retained state; use the
separate supported **Cancel backup** control for an active backup. It does not
cancel an active restore. A failure during read-only verification does not stop applications.
Before live replacement, DUMB attempts to resume any writers it stopped if the
operation fails. Once replacement has started, or if the previous running set
cannot be safely resumed, DUMB keeps applications blocked for recovery instead
of starting them against a mixture of old and restored data. Use the offered
rollback/recovery action and retain its files until recovery completes.

For a failed installation backup, **Finish backup recovery** continues the
retained service/startup recovery. The original application data remains in
place: this action does not install applications or restore an archive. Follow
any container-restart instruction before expecting services to resume. If the
archive was already verified and saved, its receipt remains available through
this recovery; an application-startup failure does not invalidate that archive.
Older
frontends label this same guarded action **Rollback**; the displayed
job-specific confirmation is still required. For a restore, **Request reviewed rollback**
instead returns the retained application state from before live replacement.
After an instructed restart, refresh status; a recovered job can still show the
failed backup's historical error without indicating another failure.

A change during a cold archive means the stopped-state assumptions were not
met. DUMB also checks the complete source again after streaming. If that final
check fails, the job error identifies a representative added, removed or changed
path, naming the metadata fields that changed or indicating changed file
contents. This is a limited sample, not a complete list of changes. Paths are
escaped for display; field values, file contents and checksums are not included
in the diagnostic.

Retain the path and job error, then identify what can still write to that path,
including another container or host process sharing the directory. Resolve the
actual writer before requesting a fresh preview and backup. An older generic
error alone cannot identify the changed entry or its writer. The failed output
is not a verified backup; do not delete state or edit the job to force acceptance.
Follow the service-resume or recovery guidance above. An operation still marked
queued or running is not eligible for rollback, even if its displayed stage or
error indicates failure. If it cannot reach a terminal recovery state, preserve
its records and request diagnosis.

## Startup and private recovery state

DUMB checks its local installation-recovery records before normal applications
start. If those records require recovery or cannot be trusted, only the API and
already-installed frontend start. Service actions can return `409` while this
installation-wide hold is active; the recovery banner identifies the blocked
controller rather than an individual application's startup failure.

Normal sign-in, session refresh and stateless session verification remain
available during this hold. A held service/setup request does not itself mean
that the browser's credentials expired. Use the retained recovery details
through direct frontend/API access; unrelated configuration and service
mutations remain blocked.

Newer frontends recognize this installation hold during the normal
post-login/onboarding check and open **Settings → Backups and restore**. This
does not mark onboarding complete or perform rollback. With an older frontend,
open and reload `/settings#backups` directly to reach that recovery entry;
normal login is still required. Unrelated API or authentication errors retain
their own diagnostics.

Some configuration mounts give new directories a group-inheritance bit
(**SGID**), even when DUMB creates them with private `0700` permissions. Current
builds recognize that inheritance on otherwise private, eligible controller
state and clear it after a complete safety check. New installation-control
folders are created with controller ownership and mode `0700`. This repair does
not make shared or writable recovery payloads trustworthy: unexpected owners,
shared/special file permissions, links and changed mounts still require review.
The diagnostic distinguishes ownership, permission and mount failures.

Preserve `/config/installation-backups`, its job records and referenced backups
when investigating a hold. Use the relevant retained recovery action, then
restart when instructed. Do not delete the directory, purge databases or apply
recursive ownership/permission changes to clear the banner. A
[major InfiniDysk migration](infinidysk-v2-migration.md#progress-cancellation-and-recovery)
has its own job, cancellation and rollback flow.

## Related tools

- [Symlink operations](symlinks.md) provides smaller link snapshots and schedules.
- [InfiniDysk 2 installation and upgrade](infinidysk-v2-migration.md) has its own
  major-upgrade archive and rollback workflow.
- Application-native backup/export tools and external systems keep their own
  recovery contracts.

# Media Library Protection

Media Library Protection reduces the chance that Plex, Jellyfin, or Emby interprets a temporary storage outage as deleted media. It is **enabled by default** and can be disabled globally or per media server.

The feature covers DUMB-managed storage dependencies such as rclone, InfiniDysk, Decypharr, Zurg, AltMount, and CLI Debrid. DUMB maps each operation to affected media servers through configured mount paths; when it cannot safely narrow the relationship, it protects every enabled media server.

!!! important "Protection is not a backup"

    This feature reduces outage risk but cannot reverse an application database change that already occurred. Keep media-server database/config backups, and avoid exposing the media server directly to mount paths that can disappear without warning.



<div class="docs-dev-section" markdown="1">

<p class="docs-dev-section-label">Development update · not in the released 2.23.0 docs</p>

New policies created by arrangement setup stay disabled until you review their mount scope and enable them deliberately. Existing policies retain their settings.

</div>



## Planned stop, restart, or update

Before DUMB changes a storage dependency it:

1. checks active playback and library-scan activity;
2. temporarily disables automatic scan triggers and cancels a running scan where the API supports it;
3. stops an idle media server for the safest maintenance path;
4. performs the storage operation;
5. waits for the dependency and mounts to remain healthy for the configured stabilization period; and
6. restores only the scan settings and media-server processes DUMB changed.

Scheduled updates use this safe policy automatically. If playback is active or activity cannot be determined, the update is deferred.

For a manual operation, dmbdb always shows the choice before DUMB pauses or stops a downstream media server:

| Choice | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Protect & continue** | Guard scans, stop an idle media server, perform the operation, then recover automatically. Available only when activity is known idle/stopped. |
| **Keep server running** | Guard scans but leave the media server running. Existing playback may still fail if it needs data no longer available from the mount. |
| **Stop now & continue** | Stop the media server immediately and continue. This explicitly interrupts active streams. |
| **Defer operation** | Make no lifecycle change. Recommended while playback is active or activity is unknown. |

## Unexpected crash or outage

When a managed storage dependency exits unexpectedly, DUMB guards downstream scans as quickly as possible. Active streams are preserved. If **Stop after users become idle during an outage** is enabled, DUMB stops that media server only after its sessions naturally finish.

After the dependency restarts and remains healthy, the recovery journal restores scan settings and restarts only media servers that DUMB stopped. The journal is stored at `/config/media-protection/state.json` with mode `0600`, so a DUMB restart does not discard an active recovery state.

## Media-server setup

1. Open the Plex, Jellyfin, or Emby service page and select **Tools → Library Protection**.
2. Review the policy for that exact server and its affected storage. For Jellyfin/Emby, enter the API key described below if setup is required.
3. Select **Save protection** and wait for **Saved**.
4. Reopen the panel and check its current protection/activity status. Resolve **Setup required** before relying on unattended maintenance.

### Plex

DUMB uses the Plex token it already manages for Plex integration. No second key is required.

The panel also exposes live Plex library preferences:

| Plex setting | Recommended | Why |
|---|---:|---|
| **Empty trash automatically after every scan** | Off | Highest-risk option: an outage-triggered scan can turn unavailable items into permanent removals. |
| **Scan my library automatically** | Off for remote/virtual mounts | Reconnect and filesystem events can be misleading. |
| **Run a partial scan when changes are detected** | On if automatic detection remains enabled | Limits the scan scope. |
| **Update libraries periodically** | Off unless supervised | A scheduled scan can overlap an unattended outage. |
| **Scan interval** | Deployment-specific | Used only when periodic updates remain enabled. |

Select **Save Plex settings** after changing these controls, then check the saved values. These controls write directly to Plex. The outage guard snapshots the current values and restores them after recovery; it does not permanently replace the choices saved in the panel.

### Jellyfin and Emby

If the application account and key are not configured, finish the media server's native first-run setup, create a dedicated API key, and paste it into **Library Protection**. Do not assume that a running process means this API authorization is ready.

The key is needed to inspect current sessions, identify and stop a running library scan, temporarily remove scheduled scan triggers, and disable/restore real-time monitoring for each virtual library.

The key is stored in `dumb.media_protection.services`, redacted from DUMB config/API responses and logs, and never sent to the browser after saving. Without a key, DUMB reports **Setup required**, treats activity as unknown, and defers safe unattended maintenance. An operator can still choose an explicit manual override.

<details class="geek-details" markdown="1">
<summary>Technical alternative: media-protection configuration and mount mapping</summary>

## Configuration

```json
{
  "dumb": {
    "media_protection": {
      "enabled": true,
      "recovery_stabilization_seconds": 30,
      "recovery_timeout_seconds": 180,
      "monitor_interval_seconds": 5,
      "services": [
        {
          "process_name": "Jellyfin Media Server",
          "enabled": true,
          "api_key": "REDACTED",
          "stop_when_idle_on_outage": true,
          "protected_mounts": ["/mnt/debrid"]
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

`protected_mounts` is optional. Leave it empty to use DUMB's dependency and `wait_for_mounts` mapping. Use explicit roots when one media server consumes only a subset of several independent mounts.
</details>

## Recovery and troubleshooting

- **Operation keeps deferring:** activity is busy or unknown. End the stream, configure the Jellyfin/Emby key, or use an explicit manual override.
- **Unused storage services:** disabled services do not open new protection incidents. DUMB automatically retires completed-operation recovery records for disabled or removed targets only when no scan snapshot, server stop, guard error, or interrupted operation is recorded. Records with possible side effects remain available for recovery.
- **Protection was disabled:** this prevents new guards and later idle-stop actions; it does not discard existing scan snapshots or restart servers while storage is unavailable.
- **Protection remains active:** verify the storage process, application health probe, mount state, and directory access. Recovery begins only after all checks remain healthy for the stabilization period.
- **Media server was not restarted:** DUMB restarts only a server it stopped. A server that was already stopped remains stopped.
- **Settings were not restored:** review the active incident and DUMB logs. API authentication or a changed/deleted library can prevent restoration and produces a critical recovery notification.
- **A stream failed under Keep server running:** scan protection does not cache media bytes. Playback still depends on the mount/provider being able to serve uncached ranges.

Because an unexpected process crash and mount disappearance can be nearly simultaneous, outage guarding is best-effort. Planned maintenance provides the strongest guarantee because DUMB applies the guard before stopping the dependency.

Source: https://dumbarr.com/dev/features/metrics/

# Metrics Collection

Use Metrics to inspect CPU, memory, filesystems, networks, and managed processes. History is enabled by default; Database Health and Plex Cloud Status are separate opt-in collectors.

---

## Check resource use in the dashboard

1. Open **Metrics** from the sidebar. Check that its connection indicator is connected and current values are changing.
2. Compare CPU and memory gauges with recent history. A brief peak is different from usage that remains high.
3. Open **Settings → Monitored Filesystems** on the Metrics page and choose the storage paths you actually use inside DUMB. Choose network interfaces under **Monitored Network Interfaces**.
4. Select **Apply** and check that the expected filesystem/interface names appear. A host path must be mounted into DUMB before it can be monitored.
5. If a resource stays high, inspect the per-process table and open the relevant service's logs before changing limits or restarting it.

Use [the Metrics page guide](../frontend/metrics.md) for chart controls, browser alerts, and optional Database Health. Backend [notifications](notifications.md) are configured separately and can work without an open browser.

## Overview

The metrics system provides:

- **Real-time monitoring** - Live CPU, memory, disk, and network stats
- **Historical tracking** - Time-series data storage for trend analysis
- **Per-process metrics** - Resource usage by individual service
- **Optional database health** - Per-service SQL and persistent-store pressure indicators
- **Optional Plex cloud status** - Cached public Plex service health, incidents, and maintenance

![Metrics overview](../assets/images/features/metrics.png){ .shadow }

---

## Collected metrics

### System metrics

| Category | Metrics |
|----------|---------|
| **CPU** | Usage %, core count, load averages (1/5/15 min) |
| **Memory** | Total, used, available, percentage |
| **Swap** | Total, used, percentage |
| **Filesystems** | Total, used, free, percentage for each selected container-visible path |
| **Inodes** | Total, used, free, percentage for each selected filesystem |
| **Network** | Bytes/packets, errors, drops, link state, speed, and MTU for selected visible interfaces |
| **System** | Boot time, uptime |

### Per-process metrics

| Metric | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **PID** | Process identifier |
| **CPU %** | Process CPU utilization |
| **Memory %** | Process memory utilization |
| **Memory RSS** | Resident set size in bytes |
